# Draft:King Magnus's Testament

]]
'King Magnus's Testament' (Rukopisanie Magnuša, korolja svejskago'', "The Manuscript of Magnus, King of Sweden") is an Old East Slavic text preserved in several Russian chronicles. It takes the form of an apocryphal first-person testament of King Magnus Eriksson, who reigned as King of Sweden and Norway during the 14th century.
The narrative focuses on Magnus's crusade against Novgorod in 1347–1351, presented as a sinful violation of the 1323 treaty. Following his defeat, the text depicts Magnus's later life as a succession of disasters sent as punishment from God. The Testament claims Magnus miraculously survived the shipwreck in 1374 and was rescued by monks from the Monastery of the Holy Saviour (Valaam Monastery). The account concludes with Magnus converting to the Orthodox faith as a schema-monk and spending his final days urging his descendants never to attack Russia again.
The text was likely composed in Novgorod between the late 14th and early 15th centuries. It survives in several versions, with the earliest ones included in the Sofia First Chronicle and the Novgorod Fourth Chronicle.
Content
The Testament is framed as a first-person monologue by King Magnus Eriksson, who exhorts his "children, brothers and the whole Swedish land" never to violate the "cross-kissing" oath by attacking Rus'. Its first half provides a brief chronicle-style survey of Swedish–Russian conflicts, beginning with the 1240 Neva campaign, in which Birger Jarl was defeated by Aleksandr Nevsky. The Testament is the only source naming Birger as the leader of this expedition. The expedition of the regent Tyrgils Knutsson is also mentioned under the name Maskalko (from Swedish marskalk, "marshal").
The second half of the Testament gives a semi-legendary account of King Magnus's life, focusing on his failed crusade against Novgorod in 1348–1351. Before the campaign, Magnus proposes a religious debate between Orthodox and Catholic faiths, which the Novgorodians reject. Scholars relate this episode to one of Saint Birgitta's visions, that Magnus appears to have followed. Magnus briefly captures Nöteborg (Orekhov) but it is soon retaken, and a second expedition ends in flight and shipwreck near the Narva River. The Testament is the only source explicitly stating Magnus undertook two separate expeditions during this crusade. Some details are independently confirmed by the  in the Swedish Rhymed Chronicle and the Novgorod Fourth Chronicle.
The remainder of narrative depicts Magnus's life as a series of disasters: Sweden suffers from flood, plague, hunger, and civil war; God takes away Magnus's sanity; he is imprisoned for one year, chained to a wall. His son Haakon ("Sakun") then takes him to Norway. There, Magnus is shipwrecked, and his men drown. Instead of drowning, the Testament claims Magnus miraculously survived:
}} Magnus is said to have lived three more days and nights, during which he wrote the Testament, explaining that God punished him for his "self-conceit" in attacking Rus'.
Date of composition and sources
The earliest surviving manuscripts containing the Testament are copies of the Sofia First Chronicle and the Novgorod Fourth Chronicle, generally dated to the second half of the 15th century; these compilations themselves are believed to have been made in the first half of the 15th century. The Testament was probably composed no later than the first quarter of the 15th century. The Moscow (Sofia) redaction typically presents an all-Russian perspective, combining accounts from various regional chronicles, while the Novgorod redaction offers a more local view.
The Testament's inclusion in both chronicles indicates that it was already included in their common protograph. The absence from the Novgorod First Chronicle suggests that it was composed specifically for an all-Russian compilation that promoted the unification of Russian principalities against external enemies.
Magnus's grave at Valaam monastery
The Valaam Monastery, situated in the Valaam Archipelago in Lake Ladoga, is the only Holy Saviour's Monastery known in that region. By the late 16th century, it was explicitly linked to the defense of the Neva region against the Swedes in the Illuminated Chronicle's account of 1240. The term "Polna River" appears across medieval Russian sources for Fennoscandian localities and likely denotes complex archipelago water systems (e.g., Åbo–Åland, Saimaa).
The Valaam Monastery was founded under Archbishop Ioann II (1388–1415) amid Swedish-backed colonization from Savo toward Ladoga. Novgorod's church and civil authorities turned Valaam into a mission base to integrate Karelians to Orthodoxy and Novgorod, at times with coercise measures.  The modern historiographical image of Valaam as ancient was largely constructed in the 19th century using heterogeneous material (chronicles, hagiographies, legends, and forgeries).
The Testament has some features of a hagiographic text (miraculous journey, salvation through monastic tonsure). After 1715, Valaam monks claimed Magnus was buried there. Lind shows this legend was likely not derived directly from the Testament but from local tradition predating 1611; early inscriptions even gave dates drawn from Olof von Dalin's history, not the Testament. There is no medieval Russian evidence that Magnus was venerated as a saint.
Comparison with other texts
The text contains historical details about Sweden that are absent from other Russian sources. Igor Shaskolsky argued these may derive from oral reports by Swedish or Gotlandic merchants at Novgorod's Gothic Yard. John H. Lind has identified parallels with the Visby Chronicle, including a one-year imprisonment (1360–1361) and a detail of Magnus being pulled ashore—which possibly inspired the Russian monks motif. The Testament also presents real historical events (Landskrona 1300; Nöteborg Treaty 1323; Magnus's 1348 capture of Nöteborg and its recapture by Novgorod).
The theme of defense of Rus' links the Testament to other early 15th-century Russian works, such as Zadonshchina and The Tale of the Battle with Mamai. The icon "The Miracle of the Icon of God's Mother of the Sign" (mid-15th c.) similarly mobilized Novgorodian resistance, casting Aleksandr Nevsky and other saints as champions—parallel to turning King Magnus into a cautionary voice against future Swedish aggression.
Later manuscript traditions show development of the text. The Nikon Chronicle presents what can be considered a second redaction, which changed the title to "Last Will of Magnus, King of Sweden" and included new dramatic episodes. Lind discusses the Valamo legend's later independence from the Testament and its local tradition roots before 1611. This version adds emotional and expressive elements, such as detailed descriptions of Magnus's physical deterioration (his eyes "as if fallen into a pit," his skin "stuck to his bones," his voice "like exhausted bees") and his son Sakun's grief upon finding him. The Nikon version also expands Magnus's confession of vices ("pride, cunning, sinfulness") and explains his attack on Rus' as an attempt to convert the local population to Catholicism. These additions give the text a more literary character with emotional-expressive sound, in contrast to earlier versions that maintained the style of an official document.
Translations
The Testament has been edited and translated in several modern languages. These include Matthias Akiander's Swedish translation of the expanded Nikon redaction (1849), John H. Lind's Danish translation of the Novgorod (Karamzin) redaction (2001), Andrej Scheglov's annotated Swedish translation of the Moscow (Sofia) redaction (2021), and N. S. Demkova's modern Russian translation with commentary (1981). The Old East Slavic manuscript tradition has also been analyzed in critical studies by Atsuo Nakazawa.
